package_info.package_manager: Windows DLL (manual dropper, not a package manager)
package_info.package_versions: Samples from Nov 2022 and Dec 2022 (hashes provided)
package_info.why_malicious: CatB is a ransomware family that encrypts user files across multiple drives, prepends ransom notes to each encrypted file, and demands a high ransom for decryption. It uses anti-analysis techniques, DLL sideloading, and manipulates system services to evade detection and ensure execution, causing significant disruption and data loss.

execution_context.trigger: runtime (initial execution of dropper DLL via rundll32.exe)
execution_context.file_location: Packed dropper DLL (UPX-packed), executed via rundll32.exe

malicious_snippets.code_language: C/C++ (pseudocode, as actual code not shown)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code checks the number of processors, available RAM, and physical disk geometry using DeviceIoControl to evade execution in virtualized or sandboxed environments, exiting if criteria are not met.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Anti-VM and anti-sandbox checks are commonly used by malware to avoid detection and analysis.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software rarely checks for processor count, RAM, and disk geometry to decide whether to run.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some high-performance or hardware-specific applications may check system specs, but not to evade analysis.
key_indicators: Multiple hardware environment checks before payload execution
Immediate process exit if checks fail

// Pseudocode for payload drop
write_file('C:\windows\system32\oci.dll', payload_dll_bytes);
malicious_snippets.code_language: C/C++ (pseudocode, as actual code not shown)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, after passing anti-VM checks, the code writes a malicious DLL payload as 'oci.dll' into the system32 directory.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Writing a DLL to system32 is a privileged operation and is a common technique for persistence or DLL hijacking.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate installers rarely drop DLLs into system32 without user consent or clear purpose.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: System updates or legitimate installers may update DLLs, but not with obfuscated or malicious payloads.
key_indicators: Filename matches a legitimate Oracle DLL (oci.dll), indicating intent to hijack

malicious_snippets.code_language: C/C++ (pseudocode, as actual code not shown)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code changes the MSDTC service to run as LocalSystem and starts it, causing the service to load the malicious oci.dll via DLL sideloading.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Changing a service to run as LocalSystem and leveraging DLL sideloading is a known privilege escalation and persistence technique.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal software does not alter system service accounts or intentionally hijack DLL loading.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Rarely, legitimate installers may reconfigure services, but not for DLL hijacking.
key_indicators: Triggering DLL sideloading via system service

malicious_snippets.code_language: C/C++ (pseudocode, as actual code not shown)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the payload enumerates files on all mounted drives (C-I), skips system files, encrypts user files, and prepends a ransom note to each encrypted file.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Mass file encryption and ransom note insertion are definitive ransomware behaviors.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not encrypt user files or demand ransom.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: No legitimate use for this behavior.
key_indicators: Enumerates and encrypts files across multiple drives
Prepends ransom note to each file
Skips system files to maintain system operability

attack_chain.action: Dropper DLL is executed via rundll32.exe, unpacking itself and starting anti-VM checks.
attack_chain.leads_to: If checks pass, proceeds to payload deployment.

attack_chain.action: Dropper writes malicious payload DLL (oci.dll) to system32 directory.
attack_chain.leads_to: Prepares for DLL sideloading via system service.

attack_chain.action: Dropper manipulates MSDTC service to run as LocalSystem and starts it, causing the service to load the malicious oci.dll.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious payload DLL is executed in the context of the service.

attack_chain.action: Malicious oci.dll payload enumerates and encrypts user files, prepending ransom notes.
attack_chain.leads_to: Files are encrypted and ransom is demanded.

behavioral_signatures: Anti-VM and anti-sandbox checks (processor, RAM, disk geometry) before payload execution
Writing DLLs to system32 directory with names matching legitimate system DLLs (e.g., oci.dll)
Manipulation of Windows services to run as LocalSystem and trigger DLL sideloading
Mass file encryption with ransom note prepended to each file
network_indicators: No C2 or web portal; ransom note contains Proton Mail address and Bitcoin wallet
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for DLLs written to system32 with names matching legitimate system DLLs (e.g., oci.dll), especially following execution of rundll32.exe with unusual DLLs. Detect anti-VM checks by monitoring for DeviceIoControl calls with IOCTL_DISK_GET_DRIVE_GEOMETRY and querying system hardware. Alert on manipulation of MSDTC or other services to run as LocalSystem and on mass file modifications where a ransom note is prepended. Use file hashes and behavioral signatures to identify known CatB components.
